stem: What is the central Jewish statement of faith, taken from Deuteronomy 6:4-9?

options.content: The Shema
options.rationale: Correct: it declares that the Lord is one.

options.content: The Kaddish
options.rationale: The Kaddish is a prayer said by mourners.

options.content: The Haggadah
options.rationale: The Haggadah is the book used at the Passover seder.

options.content: The Yigdal
options.rationale: The Yigdal is a hymn based on Maimonides' principles.

explanation: The **Shema** (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) declares the oneness of God and is recited morning and evening.

options.content: Teaching or instruction
options.rationale: Correct: Torah means teaching.

options.content: Covenant or solemn agreement
options.rationale: A covenant is a brit.

options.content: World to come
options.rationale: The world to come is olam ha-ba.

options.content: Anointed one
options.rationale: The anointed one is the mashiach (Messiah).

explanation: **Torah** means "teaching" or "instruction". In a narrow sense it is the five books of Moses.

stem: Which belief about God is central to Judaism?

options.content: God appears in three persons as Father, Son and Spirit
options.rationale: That is the Christian belief in the Trinity, not a Jewish one.

options.content: God is one of several gods, each ruling a different nation
options.rationale: Judaism teaches that there is only one God.

options.content: There is only one God, who is the creator
options.rationale: Correct: monotheism is the core belief.

options.content: God can be represented by statues in the synagogue
options.rationale: Jews do not make images of God.

explanation: Jews believe in **one God**, the creator, who has no body and is not represented by images.

stem: What do most Jews mean when they say that Jews are the "chosen people"?

options.content: They are better than every other nation in the world
options.rationale: Most Jews explain it as responsibility, not superiority.

options.content: Only they can be saved and all other peoples are condemned
options.rationale: Judaism teaches that righteous people of all nations have a share in the world to come.

options.content: They may not take part in the life of other communities
options.rationale: Chosenness is not a rule about separation.

options.content: They have been given responsibilities under the covenant
options.rationale: Correct: being chosen means duty, not superiority.

explanation: Being **chosen** means being asked to keep the Torah and live by God's ways. It is a responsibility, not a claim of superiority.

options.content: A shawl with fringes worn by Jews at morning prayer
options.rationale: That is the tallit.

options.content: A cap worn by Jewish men as a sign of respect for God
options.rationale: That is the kippah.

options.content: A small case with the Shema, fixed to a doorpost
options.rationale: Correct: it follows the command in Deuteronomy 6:9.

options.content: A scroll of the Torah read aloud in the synagogue
options.rationale: That is the Sefer Torah.

explanation: The **mezuzah** is a small case on the doorpost containing the verses of the Shema. It reminds the family of God's presence.

stem: Nyasha reads that some Jews expect a personal Messiah while others speak of a messianic age. What does this show about Judaism?

options.content: Jews no longer share any beliefs about the future of the world
options.rationale: The hope for a time of peace is widely shared.

options.content: Jews share a hope for a time of peace but understand it in different ways
options.rationale: Correct: the hope is shared; the interpretation differs.

options.content: Only Orthodox Jews are regarded as Jews by other Jewish groups
options.rationale: Jews of all groups are Jews; the groups differ on belief and practice.

options.content: Judaism believes that the Messiah has already come, but some Jews doubt it
options.rationale: Jews believe that the Messiah has not yet come.

explanation: Many **Orthodox** Jews expect a personal Messiah; many **Reform** Jews speak of a messianic age. Both hope for peace and justice.
hints: Think of the words many Orthodox and many Reform.

stem: Which statement about Jewish belief in life after death is the most accurate?

options.content: All Jews teach exactly the same detailed account of life after death
options.rationale: Jewish views vary.

options.content: Judaism teaches that nothing is known and nobody thinks about life after death
options.rationale: Many Jews do believe in olam ha-ba.

options.content: Judaism teaches that people are reborn many times in new bodies in this world
options.rationale: Rebirth in this world is not the traditional Jewish teaching.

options.content: Jews hold different views, including the world to come and resurrection
options.rationale: Correct: views vary among Jews.

explanation: Many traditional Jews believe in **olam ha-ba** and the **resurrection of the dead**; others stress the soul or this life. Judaism emphasises how one lives.
hints: Remember that Judaism puts most weight on this life.

stem: Which pair of qualities of God do Jews hold together, as shown on Yom Kippur?

options.content: Anger and revenge
options.rationale: Judaism does not describe God in these terms as God's main qualities.

options.content: Silence and distance
options.rationale: Jews believe God is close and hears prayer.

options.content: Justice and mercy
options.rationale: Correct: God is just, yet merciful to those who repent.

options.content: Power and secrecy
options.rationale: Power is part of belief in God, but the pair asked about is justice and mercy.

explanation: On Yom Kippur Jews trust that God is **just** and **merciful** and will forgive those who sincerely repent.
hints: On the Day of Atonement Jews ask for forgiveness.

stem: Jews believe that God is one.
explanation: True. This is the message of the Shema.

stem: Judaism teaches that the Messiah has already come.
explanation: False. Jews are still waiting for the Messiah. This is a difference between Judaism and Christianity, and should be stated respectfully.

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: the declaration that the Lord is one
the anointed one expected to bring peace and justice

explanation: Shema: oneness of God. Mashiach: Messiah. Olam ha-ba: world to come. Brit: covenant.

payload.template: The Shema is found in the Book of {{blank:a}}, chapter {{blank:b}}.
The Thirteen Principles of Faith were written by {{blank:a}}, a scholar who lived in the {{blank:b}} century CE.

explanation: **Maimonides** (Rambam) set out thirteen principles in the **twelfth** century CE.
hints: He is also known as the Rambam.

stem: What is the Hebrew term for "the world to come"?
explanation: **Olam ha-ba** means the world to come.

stem: Identify **three** things that Jews do to show their belief in one God.

points.description: Recite the Shema morning and evening
Fix a mezuzah on the doorposts of the home
Pray, wear tefillin in the weekday morning prayer, or keep the Sabbath

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Jews recite the Shema in the morning and the evening, fix a mezuzah on the doorposts of the home, and pray daily, wearing tefillin at weekday morning prayer.

stem: Describe what Jews mean by the idea that they are the chosen people.

points.description: They believe God made a covenant with the Jewish people
They were given the Torah and its commandments
Being chosen means responsibility to live by God's ways
It does not mean that they are better than other peoples

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Jews believe that God made a covenant with the Jewish people and gave them the Torah and its commandments. Being chosen means responsibility to live by God's ways. It does not mean that Jews are better than other peoples.

hints: Say what was given, what it asks of Jews and what it does not mean.

stem: Explain **two** ways in which belief in one God affects the daily life of Jews.

points.description: They recite the Shema each morning and evening
Developed: this repeated declaration reminds them every day that God is one and that they must love God
They fix a mezuzah on the doorposts
Developed: it reminds the family at each doorway of God's presence and the commandments, as taught in Deuteronomy 6

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Jews recite the Shema each morning and evening, which reminds them every day that God is one and that they must love God with all their heart. They also fix a mezuzah on the doorposts, which reminds the family each time they pass of God's presence and of the commandments, as taught in Deuteronomy 6.

explanation: Two ways, each stated (1) and developed (2 across the way).
hints: Choose two practices and link each to the belief.

stem:
**Source A** — a conversation between two fictional students, a Jewish student and a Christian student, in a school in Gweru, 2026 (invented for this question)

> Rachel: At home my family says the Shema at night. It says that God is one, and that we must teach it to our children.
> Tatenda: In my church we say that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Do Jews also expect the Messiah?
> Rachel: Yes, we are still waiting for him. Some of us expect a person from King David's family; some of us talk about a time of peace for the whole world.

Study Source A and answer the questions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: According to Source A, what do Jews say in the Shema?

options.content: That God is in three persons
options.rationale: Tatenda describes the Christian belief; it is not the Shema.

options.content: That God is one
options.rationale: Correct: Rachel says the Shema states that God is one.

options.content: That the Messiah has already come
options.rationale: Rachel says Jews are still waiting.

options.content: That the Torah may be changed
options.rationale: The source does not say this.

parts.explanation: Rachel states the key point of the Shema: God is one.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Using Source A, state **three** things Jews believe or do.

points.description: They say the Shema at night
They believe God is one
They are still waiting for the Messiah, understood in different ways

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Jews say the Shema at night, believe that God is one, and are still waiting for the Messiah, whom some expect to be a person from David's family and others understand as a time of peace.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the beliefs in Source A show both agreement and difference between Judaism and Christianity.

points.description: Both believe in one God, creator and the Messiah as a hope
Christians believe God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, while Jews do not
Jews are still waiting for the Messiah, while Christians believe he has come in Jesus

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Both religions believe in one God. Christians describe God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, which Jews do not teach, and Jews are still waiting for the Messiah while Christians believe that the Messiah has come in Jesus.

explanation: The source gives the Shema, the divine unity and the expectation of the Messiah.
hints: In (c) state one point of agreement and two differences, written respectfully.

stem: Miriam says: "Belief in one God is the most important teaching of Judaism." Her friend Farai says: "Keeping the commandments matters more than belief."

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Outline **two** teachings of Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith.

points.description: God exists and is the creator, and is one
God has no body and is eternal
The Torah is from God and will not be changed (or Moses was the greatest prophet)
God rewards and punishes justly, and the Messiah will come

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: God exists, is the creator and is one; God has no body and is eternal. The Torah is from God and will not be changed. God rewards and punishes justly and the Messiah will come.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why many Orthodox and Reform Jews understand the Torah differently.

points.description: Many Orthodox Jews believe that the whole Torah was given by God and that its commandments remain binding
Many Reform Jews believe that it is inspired by God but that each generation interprets how to apply it

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Many Orthodox Jews believe that the whole Torah was given by God and that its commandments remain binding. Many Reform Jews believe that it is inspired by God but that each generation must interpret how to apply it.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Assess the view that belief in one God matters more than keeping the commandments in Judaism.

points.description: For belief: the Shema begins everything, and the commandments are given by the one God
For action: Jewish life is shaped by practice (Sabbath, food laws, charity), and the prophets stress justice
Link: in Judaism belief and practice are joined; the Shema itself tells Jews to love God and to keep the words in daily life
A supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Belief in one God is the foundation of Judaism, since the Shema begins everything and the commandments are given by the one God. Yet Jewish life is shaped by practice, such as the Sabbath, food laws and charity, and the prophets stress justice above ritual. In Judaism the two cannot easily be separated: the Shema tells Jews both to love God and to keep these words in daily life. I conclude that belief matters first, but that it is shown through action.

explanation: A strong answer weighs both claims and notes that the Shema joins belief and action.
hints: Present both views, then show how belief and practice are linked.
